content: The oxeye daisy, scientifically known as Leucanthemum vulgare (synonym Chrysanthemum leucanthemum), is a flowering plant native to Europe and temperate regions of Asia. It is commonly referred to by several names, including marguerite, moon daisy, and dog daisy. This plant is a perennial herb that grows prostrate, with flower heads that do not exceed 5 cm in diameter. Each flower head is composed of approximately 20 white ray florets surrounding numerous yellow disc florets, which are located at the terminal end of the stem. The stem is typically unbranched and grows laterally from a creeping rootstock. The leaves of the oxeye daisy are dark green on both sides. The basal and middle leaves are petiolate, obovate to spoon-shaped, and have serrated or dentate edges. In contrast, the upper leaves are shorter, sessile, and grow directly along the stem. The plant produces a large number of flat seeds that lack a pappus. Additionally, it propagates vegetatively through its underground stems, which root and give rise to new plants. The oxeye daisy is a characteristic flower of meadows and is found in diverse plant communities, including dry fields, meadows, areas under shrubs, open-canopy forests, and even waste sites. It is highly adaptable to various environmental conditions and thrives particularly well in heavy, damp soils. This species has been introduced to regions such as North America, Australia, and New Zealand, where it has become a common weed. In some areas, it displaces native plant species, making it an invasive species. Its eradication is challenging because new plants can regenerate from fragments of its rhizomes. Despite its invasive nature, in North Carolina, the oxeye daisy is intentionally planted along roadsides by the highway department. The unopened flower buds of the oxeye daisy can be marinated and used as a culinary ingredient, similar to capers. This flower is also famously associated with the game He loves me, he loves me not, known in French as effeuiller la marguerite.
